title: Training the Teacher Who Understands Both Sides
source_title: China's first bachelor's program in AI education to address teacher shortage
source_verification: URL可访问；核验了项目定位、技术与教育双模块、伦理和数据安全课程及协作实践模式。
adaptation_note: 题材参考所列权威来源的公开事实；本站原创改写，非媒体原文，非历年真题。
content:
A school can buy an AI tool in a day, but preparing a teacher to use it well takes much longer. Beijing Normal University launched an undergraduate program in AI education because schools need people who understand both the technology and the classroom.

The course design joins two kinds of knowledge. Students study machine learning, natural language processing and educational data. They also learn psychology, learning theory, lesson design and assessment. This combination matters because a technically impressive tool may still be unsuitable for a child's age or a lesson's purpose. Meanwhile, a skilled classroom teacher cannot examine an AI system's limits without some technical understanding.

The program includes AI ethics and data security as required subjects. It also plans practical courses and cooperation among the university, companies and schools. Such cooperation is interdisciplinary: it brings knowledge from different fields together around one problem. Students can therefore test ideas in real teaching settings instead of treating education as a simple market for new software.

Graduates may become AI teachers, develop learning platforms, conduct research or help shape policy. These paths differ, but they share one principle: technology should serve education. The program's real answer to the teacher shortage is not merely to produce more AI specialists. It is to prepare specialists who can ask what learning needs before deciding what a machine should do.

title: An AI School as a Campus Experiment
source_title: Tsinghua University to launch new school for AI talent development
source_verification: 清单URL本轮直接打开失败；经同标题检索核验到新华社可见页面（不同内容ID），确认标题、日期、约150人计划及117门试点课程、147个课堂等事实。
adaptation_note: 题材参考所列权威来源的公开事实；本站原创改写，非媒体原文，非历年真题。
content:
When a university opens a school devoted to artificial intelligence, the obvious question is how many AI experts it will produce. Tsinghua University's plan offers another question: can AI also change the way those experts are educated?

The new undergraduate school planned to enroll about 150 students in its first year. Its goal was not limited to technical training. It would combine AI with several disciplines and develop students' literacy, expertise and capacity for innovation. That design reflects a basic fact: many important uses of AI occur in medicine, engineering, science or the humanities rather than inside a single computer laboratory.

The wider university had already started testing AI in teaching. It reported 117 pilot courses and 147 classes using AI-supported methods, along with teaching assistants, lesson-planning aids and automated grading systems. These trials make the campus a kind of laboratory for the new school. Faculty members can observe where a tool saves time, where it confuses students, and where human review remains necessary. A pilot is a limited test conducted before a larger decision.

The numbers, however, should not be mistaken for proof of better learning. Counting tools or classes is easier than measuring whether students ask deeper questions or transfer knowledge across fields. The school will be most valuable if it studies its own educational experiments as carefully as it studies AI itself.

title: Opening an AI Academy Without Closing the Door
source_title: Across China: Teen AI academies pave way for China's next-gen innovators
source_verification: URL直接打开偶发内部错误；同URL搜索结果可见全文，核验了北京与上海项目、31所高校资源、科研参与及海淀项目招生数据。
adaptation_note: 题材参考所列权威来源的公开事实；本站原创改写，非媒体原文，非历年真题。
content:
Teen AI academies in Beijing and Shanghai are designed as bridges. They connect secondary schools with universities, research projects and industry practice. In Beijing, one academy planned to draw on faculty from 31 universities and let students participate in national-level research. A related Haidian program teaches computational thinking, mathematics, programming and AI fundamentals on weekends and holidays.

Such programs can offer an experience that an ordinary timetable rarely provides. A teenager may encounter an unsolved problem, work with a researcher and see how mathematics becomes a model. Early depth can be valuable, especially in a field advancing too quickly for textbooks alone.

The bridge, however, has an entrance. In 2024, the Haidian experimental class accepted 180 students after receiving more than 1,500 applications; the reported admission rate was 11.76 percent. Selectivity may help a demanding course operate, but it also raises a design question. If the public purpose is to build a broad talent pipeline, what should happen to interested students who are not selected? A pipeline is a continuing route through which learners can develop, not merely a contest that identifies a few winners.

One answer is a layered system. Intensive academies can provide research opportunities to a smaller group, while regular schools offer basic AI literacy, open projects and routes to later entry. Selection should also look for curiosity and persistence, not only prior programming experience, because earlier access to devices and tutoring is uneven.

The success of a teen academy should therefore be measured in two directions. It should help advanced learners move farther, but its methods and resources should also strengthen the wider educational path from which future applicants emerge.

title: The Smart Playground Still Needs a Teacher
source_title: Chinese schools start new semester with more AI-empowered facilities
source_verification: URL可访问；核验了智能体育场、可穿戴心率数据、英语口语反馈、184个试点基地及大班教学背景。
adaptation_note: 题材参考所列权威来源的公开事实；本站原创改写，非媒体原文，非历年真题。
content:
On a smart playground, a three-minute rope-skipping test can produce an immediate score and ranking. In another class, a wrist device reports heart rate while students exercise. Elsewhere, a small terminal comments on a learner's English pronunciation and grammar. These systems promise something teachers in large classes have always lacked: a quick view of each student's performance.

Speed, however, changes the teacher's problem rather than solving it. A heart-rate alert may signal that an exercise should be adjusted, but it does not know whether a child is ill, frightened or simply unfamiliar with the task. A pronunciation score can locate a repeated sound error, yet the teacher must decide whether correction, encouragement or more listening will help. Data become educational only after someone interprets them in context.

The scale of new facilities makes that judgment especially important. One smart playground described in the source covered 16,000 square meters and was intended to serve more than 7,000 students and 700 teachers. Nationally, 184 primary and secondary schools had been named AI education pilot bases in early 2024. A pilot base is expected to explore methods, not merely display equipment.

There are also questions that convenience can hide. Facial recognition may reduce the time needed to record performance, while creating duties concerning consent, storage and access. Instant rankings may motivate some students but embarrass others. Personalized assistance can narrow a learning gap only if devices work reliably and teachers have time to respond. Otherwise, the system produces finer descriptions of unequal outcomes without changing them.

The useful contrast is not between technology and teachers. It is between automatic measurement and informed action. Smart facilities earn their place when they give teachers better evidence, protect students and lead to decisions that a score cannot make by itself.

title: AI Literacy Is More Than Learning to Prompt
source_title: Yearender-China Focus: AI takes root in basic education, nurturing future innovators
source_verification: URL直接打开偶发内部错误；同URL搜索结果可见全文，核验了天津分层课程、北京课时、教师培训、人机边界、作业禁令与伦理风险。
adaptation_note: 题材参考所列权威来源的公开事实；本站原创改写，非媒体原文，非历年真题。
content:
Basic AI education teaches students to obtain a polished answer. A harder version asks when that answer deserves trust, what was lost in producing it, and whether using it serves the learning goal. China's school programs increasingly describe their aim as AI literacy rather than technical specialization, a distinction with consequences for curriculum, assessment and teacher preparation.

A tiered curriculum illustrates the idea. In Tianjin, fourth- and eighth-grade students were assigned one compulsory AI class each week, while other grades could use school-designed courses or integrate AI into existing subjects. Beijing required a minimum of eight AI classes per academic year, moving from experience in primary school toward application and then project work. Progression here is developmental rather than merely cumulative: older learners are expected to make more independent judgments, not simply collect more commands.

That judgment is difficult to assess. A successful program might enable a student to model a physical process, question biased output, protect personal data and explain why a tool should be refused for a particular task. None of these achievements is captured well by counting logins. Nor can schools assume that installing software creates capacity. Teachers across subjects need training, usable lesson materials and time to redesign activities; families also need enough understanding to recognize unhealthy dependence.

Boundaries make the educational purpose visible. National guidance reported in 2025 prohibited submitting AI-generated material directly as homework or exam answers and called for safeguards in creative assignments. The restriction is not anti-technology. It protects the intellectual work that an assignment is meant to reveal. Human-AI collaboration is valuable only if the human remains cognitively present—forming questions, checking claims and taking responsibility for the result.

There is nevertheless a policy tension. Broad access can reduce gaps in exposure, yet uneven devices, connectivity and teacher confidence may turn a common curriculum into unequal experiences. Moreover, privacy protection, algorithmic bias and data security are not optional advanced topics; they determine whether routine participation is safe. AI literacy should therefore be evaluated as a public capability: the capacity to use, question and sometimes decline an automated system. Teaching students to prompt is one component. Teaching them to remain authors of their decisions is the larger task.

questions.explanation: 全文把AI素养界定为使用、质疑、拒绝和承担责任的综合公共能力。
questions.evidence_text: AI literacy should therefore be evaluated as a public capability: the capacity to use, question and sometimes decline an automated system.

title: A Major Is More Than Its Name
content:
A university can announce a fashionable major in one afternoon. Building a useful course takes much longer. In 2025, China's education authorities added 29 undergraduate majors in fields including artificial intelligence, carbon neutrality and the low-altitude economy. More than 500 universities had already established AI majors or schools.

The numbers show strong interest, but a new name is not enough. Students need teachers who understand the field, equipment for practice and links with real workplaces. Otherwise, a department may simply add words such as "smart" or "digital" to an old program while leaving its lessons almost unchanged.

Vocational undergraduate institutions offer one useful test: practical training is expected to occupy about half of class time. Practice here means applying knowledge to a real or realistic task, not only remembering definitions.

New majors can help prepare a future workforce. Their value, however, should be judged by what students can actually learn and do. Employers and graduates can later reveal whether promised abilities survived outside an examination or brochure. A modern label may attract applicants; a coherent curriculum is what turns that promise into education.

title: Eight Hours, Three Stages of Learning
content:
Eight hours may sound small, but a clear starting point can change how a subject enters school. Beijing announced that primary and secondary students would receive at least eight class hours of artificial intelligence education each academic year from autumn 2025.

The content is not identical for every age. Primary pupils begin with experience and curiosity. Junior high students move toward understanding and application, while senior high students are asked to explore practice and innovation. Schools may teach a separate AI course or connect the topic with other subjects.

This progression matters. A seven-year-old and a seventeen-year-old should not face the same technical task. Progression means arranging learning so that later work builds on earlier understanding.

The annual minimum also creates a common promise: AI learning should not depend entirely on whether one school happens to have an enthusiastic club. It also gives families a visible expectation against which they can ask questions. Yet hours alone cannot guarantee quality. Teachers need suitable materials and training. The schedule opens the door; age-appropriate teaching determines what students gain after they enter.

title: Keep the Student in the Thinking Loop
content:
At a youth technology event, two eighth graders built a sign that used sensors and a small AI system to guide shoppers in a mall. They were among roughly 170,000 students who registered for the event; nearly 8,000 reached the final stage.

The project illustrates a shift from asking AI for answers to designing something with it. Some schools now ask students in grades four to nine to complete an inquiry project each semester, with at least four class periods devoted to the work. An inquiry begins with a question, tests ideas and improves a result.

That process is important because easy answers can hide weak thinking. If a learner copies a generated paragraph, the machine has completed the difficult part. If the learner compares suggestions, checks facts and explains a design choice, AI becomes a tool inside human reasoning.

Schools therefore face a simple rule: the student must remain the thinker. A successful AI project is not the one with the smoothest output. It is the one whose learner can describe the problem, the evidence and the decisions that produced it.

title: Why One Score Cannot Describe a School System
content:
Basic education is easy to describe with one score, but much harder to improve with one measure. China has about 430,000 schools and kindergartens serving around 220 million students. A system of that size must consider learning, health, character and fairness together.

Recent policy discussion has placed health and virtue beside academic development. It has also emphasized balanced compulsory education across regions. All 2,895 county-level areas had passed a national assessment of basic educational balance, and internet access had reached every school.

Access, however, is not only a cable or a school gate. Children with disabilities may need support that allows them to participate meaningfully. Their enrollment rate in compulsory education had reached 97 percent. Equity means responding to different barriers so that opportunity is genuinely usable.

These facts point to a broad definition of quality. A good school system does not merely produce high test results in a few places. It also asks whether children feel safe enough to participate and curious enough to continue. It helps many kinds of learners grow in body, judgment and knowledge. Scale makes common standards necessary; human difference makes flexible support equally necessary.

title: A Riderʼs Experience Can Lead Somewhere New
content:
Delivery riders already know traffic, time pressure and customer service. A new vocational academy in Guangdong treats that experience as a starting point rather than a dead end. Its courses include safety and workers' rights, but also AI dispatch, autonomous delivery, cold-chain operations and fleet management.

The program was created by local authorities and an online retailer. Training is voluntary, organized in levels and offered with basic tuition support from the platform. This arrangement matters because working adults cannot always leave their jobs for a long full-time course.

Other cities are testing similar connections between training and new work. Yichang ran 30 drone sessions for 606 trainees, while Baiyin offered free drone courses and job referrals. A referral is an introduction that helps a qualified learner reach an employer; it is not a guarantee of employment.

These programs broaden the meaning of vocational education. They do not ask whether a job is old or new. They ask which abilities are changing and how workers can move toward the next role. Follow-up matters as well: providers should learn whether participants completed training, used the skill and found work related to it. Without that evidence, enrollment can be mistaken for opportunity. The strongest course links familiar experience, emerging technology and a realistic path into work.

title: When a Robotics Club Outgrows the Club Room
content:
In 2017, a Tianjin middle school formed a small robotics club. Students and teachers learned largely through self-study, travelled to competitions and gradually won awards. By 2022, the activity had become an after-school program open to every student, accompanied by technology innovation courses.

That history matters more than a photograph of a robot. It shows how a school can move from an enthusiastic group to wider participation. In 2024, the school was among 184 primary and secondary AI education bases named by the Ministry of Education.

AI later appeared beyond robotics. A classroom assistant reviewed earlier lesson points and assessed English reading. Physical education teachers used machines to give feedback on middle-distance running. Integration here means placing a tool inside an existing subject for a clear learning purpose.

Expansion nevertheless creates a teacher problem. A club can depend on one specialist; a school-wide program cannot. More teachers must understand when the technology helps, how to interpret its feedback and when to ignore it. The journey from club to curriculum therefore requires institutional learning as well as student learning.

The lesson is not that every classroom needs a robot. It is that educational innovation becomes durable only when access widens, purposes become clearer and staff capacity grows with the technology too.

title: The 2030 Goal Is an Ecosystem
content:
A national “AI Plus Education” plan proposes a broad change: by 2030, AI education should extend across all stages of schooling and to the wider public. Primary and secondary schools may offer dedicated lessons, connect AI with other subjects and add hands-on activities after class.

Universities face a different task. The plan calls for basic AI learning for all students and interdisciplinary courses that combine computing with other fields. It also asks institutions to adjust majors as industries change. The goal is not to turn every learner into the same specialist, but to make technical understanding useful inside varied forms of expertise.

AI is also expected to support teachers through homework management, grading, question answering and analysis of classroom interaction. Such assistance can release time, yet it shifts rather than removes professional judgment. A pattern detected by software still needs a teacher to decide what it means for a particular class.

This is why the plan also reaches teacher qualification and certification. System-wide use requires educators who can question outputs, protect learners and choose an appropriate task. Scaling means extending a practice widely while preserving the conditions that make it responsible.

The 2030 goal should therefore be read as an ecosystem, not a shopping list of tools. Courses, disciplines, teacher preparation and classroom safeguards must develop together if wider adoption is to improve learning rather than merely increase usage.

title: The Skill That Survives a Change of Machine
content:
At a vocational workshop in Lahore, students do not learn automation from diagrams alone. They operate modern equipment and digital platforms, working with production lines, robotics and electrical systems. The program was jointly established by a Chinese college and Punjabʼs vocational training authority in 2018.

By 2025, the workshop had trained more than 1,000 students. Some graduates found work in major industries in Pakistan and abroad. Those outcomes matter, but the most useful feature is the connection between equipment, instruction and an industrial task.

Hands-on training is sometimes mistaken for repeating a fixed procedure. Genuine practice asks a learner to diagnose an error, explain a system and adjust it safely. Transfer means applying an underlying principle when the machine or workplace changes.

International cooperation adds another layer. Imported equipment can expose learners to current standards, while local teachers and employers understand the jobs, language and constraints around them. Neither side supplies a complete course alone.

A workshop should therefore be judged by more than its machines. It needs instructors who can connect theory with operation, maintenance plans that keep laboratories usable and evidence that graduates can adapt. Employers can test that adaptability over time. Modern equipment opens a door; transferable understanding allows a learner to keep walking after the first job changes.

title: A Million Books Still Need a Guide
content:
In a mountain school in Zhejiang, a reading corner used to offer only a few hundred books, many outdated or unsuitable. A pilot launched in November 2025 supplied smart terminals to small rural schools with fewer than 100 pupils. Students in grades four to six could then reach stories, poems and pronunciation support through an AI assistant.

The change addresses scarcity, but it does not make selection automatic. An endless digital shelf can overwhelm a beginner as easily as an empty shelf can restrict one. Teachers at the school shifted attention toward curating suitable materials, giving personal guidance and encouraging pupils to finish whole books. About half the students developed a daily reading habit.

Elsewhere, digital access takes different forms. On Zhejiang islands, a shared library system delivers borrowed books within two or three days. A Guizhou platform provides more than one million e-books alongside journals, lectures and audiobooks. These examples distinguish access to a catalogue from access to a reading practice.

The distinction matters because a resource becomes educational only when a learner can choose it, understand it and return to it. Curation means selecting and organizing material for a particular audience; it is not censorship of every difficult text.

Digital tools can narrow a geographical gap, yet they do not remove the need for adults who know their pupils. The best rural reading program joins abundant material with patient guidance, turning connection into a habit rather than a brief encounter with a screen.

title: The Smart Classroom After Launch Day
content:
A rural school in Shiqian, Guizhou, received an AI-powered smart classroom system in 2025. The visible report is brief: it confirms the delivery and says the system offers new learning pathways. Those modest facts are enough to raise a larger educational question. What turns installed equipment into learning?

Delivery is the easiest stage to photograph. Teachers must still decide which lesson benefits from the system, what students should do rather than merely watch, and how they will know whether understanding improved. If a device supplies an answer before a learner has formed a question, novelty may shorten rather than deepen attention.

Infrastructure is therefore an enabling condition, not an outcome. An enabling condition makes an activity possible but does not ensure its success. Electricity, connectivity and working hardware matter; so do lesson design, maintenance and local technical support. A broken system waiting months for repair creates a different classroom from the one shown on launch day.

Rural schools also need freedom to adapt. A tool designed around an urban textbook sequence may not fit local schedules, languages or examples. Teachers should be able to choose a smaller use that solves a genuine problem instead of demonstrating every available feature.

Evaluation should follow the same logic. Counting devices reveals distribution, while student work reveals use. Observations, questions and later performance can show whether the technology expands participation or simply changes the surface of a lesson.

The fair test of a smart classroom comes after the visitors leave: can teachers keep using it purposefully, and can learners explain something they could not explain before?

title: Open All Day Is Not the Same as Accessible
content:
Four hundred Chinese colleges and universities launched about 700 lifelong-learning projects in 2025. The courses, offered online and offline, covered areas such as digital technology, AI applications and rural revitalization. Intended learners included migrant workers, rural teachers and older adults.

The variety is a strength only if it survives contact with adult life. A worker with changing shifts may need a short mobile lesson; an older learner may value a nearby classroom and technical help; a rural teacher may need a course timed outside the busiest school weeks. Accessibility is not simply the existence of a course. It is the practical ability to enter, continue and benefit from it.

An online public platform launched in late 2024 with 1,000 courses in six categories, including workplace skills, hobbies, continuing education and education for older people. A broad catalogue helps learners find relevant goals, but categories alone cannot reveal whether a course is understandable, affordable or recognized by employers.

Universities can contribute more than recorded lectures. They can connect research with local problems, lend trusted assessment to short programs and provide spaces where different generations learn together. Yet their prestige should not silence feedback from participants whose schedules and barriers differ from those of full-time students.

The promise of learning “around the clock” and across all regions is therefore a design obligation. Providers must examine when people leave a course, what support they lacked and whether a new skill changed their options.

Lifelong learning succeeds not when education is technically always open, but when adults with complicated lives can repeatedly return and make progress.

title: A Future Classroom Needs a Present Tense Test
content:
At a Wuhan primary school, pupils wore virtual-reality headsets, designed Mars rescue vehicles with AI tools and made customized logos through 3D printing. The scene attracted visitors to the 2025 World Digital Education Conference because it made a “future classroom” visible.

Another room told a less dramatic story. Learners in their sixties practiced flying drones in a simulation at an open university. Elsewhere, a national platform offered more than 110,000 resources for basic education, while synchronized lessons had connected strong teachers with rural schools in Fujian.

These examples should not be collapsed into one claim that technology automatically modernizes education. The Mars project may cultivate design and teamwork; a senior course can build confidence; a shared platform can reduce distance. Each has a different learner, problem and measure of success.

The conference also heard a warning: AI creates opportunities while making academic honesty and oversight harder. Integrity means that learning evidence truthfully represents a studentʼs own understanding and effort. It requires task design, disclosure rules and teachers capable of questioning polished output.

Digital education is often presented as a ladder: more devices, more users, more intelligence. In practice it resembles a map with several destinations. Equity, creativity, efficiency and lifelong participation do not always follow the same route, and one tool may advance one goal while weakening another.

The useful question is therefore not whether a classroom looks futuristic. It is which educational purpose has been named, what evidence would show progress, and what new risk must be managed along the way.

title: A Blueprint Needs Places to Change Course
content:
Chinaʼs 2024–2035 education blueprint sets two horizons. By 2027, it expects an initial high-quality system and stronger independent talent development. By 2035, it aims for a fully developed system, broad lifelong learning and educational modernization.

Long horizons can coordinate investment, but they also create a measurement problem. A distant vision is too easy to praise if no one specifies what should be different in classrooms, teacher preparation or regional access along the way. The 2027 milestone matters because it makes the larger promise interruptible: evidence can lead to correction before 2035.

The blueprint covers basic education, higher education, vocational skill and international exchange. It calls for research universities and urgently needed interdisciplinary fields, while also stressing balanced compulsory education and demographic change. These goals may compete for staff and money. Strategic alignment means directing programs toward public needs without reducing education to short-term labor forecasts.

One example is discipline adjustment. In 2024, authorities reported adding 1,673 undergraduate programs considered important to national strategies and removing 1,670 less aligned ones. Such responsiveness can prevent permanent mismatch. Yet new fields need time for faculty and knowledge to mature, and unpopular foundational subjects may have value that current job statistics miss.

Evaluation must therefore distinguish motion from improvement. Opening a major, signing an exchange agreement or purchasing equipment records activity. Stronger teaching, fairer opportunity and better-supported inquiry are outcomes.

A blueprint earns credibility through the decisions it changes and the evidence it invites. Public reporting also lets teachers, families and institutions contest an indicator that measures the wrong outcome. Milestones should not merely celebrate distance travelled; they should reveal whether the route still leads toward the stated public purposes.

title: Beyond Sixty-One Billion Page Views
content:
By April 2025, Smart Education of China had more than 164 million registered users and 61.3 billion page views. Visitors came from over 220 countries and regions. The platform contained more than 110,000 basic-education resources, 11,300 vocational courses, 31,000 higher-education courses and 2,000 lifelong-learning offerings.

These figures establish scale, not learning. Registration shows that a person created access; a page view records contact with a page. Neither reveals whether a teacher changed a lesson, a student understood a difficult idea or an adult completed a useful course. A metric is a defined measure, and its value depends on the question it is meant to answer.

Scale still matters. A national platform can distribute scarce material cheaply, connect remote schools with strong resources and offer continuity when local courses are unavailable. Its 51 services, organized in eight categories, also extend beyond lessons to areas such as employment and examinations.

Yet abundance can shift inequality rather than remove it. Learners with weak connectivity, limited digital skills or inaccessible interfaces may receive a formal invitation but little practical benefit. Recommendation systems can help navigation, though they may also narrow what users encounter. Public platforms need accessible design, transparent selection and alternatives for low-bandwidth use.

Evaluation should therefore follow a chain. First ask who can reach the service. Then examine meaningful use: completion, return, teacher adaptation and the quality of learner work. Finally, compare outcomes across regions and groups. Large totals can coexist with systematic exclusion hidden inside averages.

The platformʼs achievement is real infrastructure. Its educational achievement must be demonstrated at a much finer resolution, where numbers are linked to what different people were able to do.

title: The Cloud Still Needs a Road to the Classroom
content:
In Zambia, a cloud-supported AI service was presented as a way to bring smart education to areas that remain underserved. Its proposed uses included personalized learning, language translation, curriculum support and real-time educational content. Government representatives placed the technology within a longer partnership on digital education.

The appeal is clear: cloud services can concentrate computing and material that one rural school could not maintain alone. A learner may receive updated content without a large local server, and translation may help a lesson cross language boundaries. Seamless, however, is an aspiration, not a description of every userʼs experience.

Cloud dependence introduces a chain of failure. A national service may operate perfectly while a village lacks stable electricity, an affordable device or reliable connectivity. Even when the connection works, a translation model may mishandle a local expression or a personalized path may be based on incomplete data. Reliability means consistent performance under the conditions in which people actually use a service.

Ownership also matters. Schools need to know where learner data travel, who can correct an error and whether local educators can adapt content. A system that is technically available but professionally opaque can weaken rather than strengthen teacher agency.

This does not cancel the promise of shared infrastructure. It clarifies the investment required around it: power, networks, device repair, teacher preparation, accessible interfaces and accountable agreements with providers. The least visible components may decide whether the most advanced feature reaches a child.

Bridging a digital divide is not the act of placing a service on one side and announcing that everyone may enter. It is the sustained work of making the entire route usable, trustworthy and educationally relevant.

title: The Five Thresholds After a Signal Arrives
content:
China reported more than 1.12 billion internet users by June 2025, with national penetration at 79.7 percent. Among people aged sixty and above, 161 million were online and penetration reached 52 percent. Rural users numbered 322 million, with a penetration rate of 69.2 percent. Fifth-generation mobile service covered more than 90 percent of administrative villages.

These numbers matter to education because connectivity is now an entrance to courses, libraries and generative AI. They also demonstrate why a national average can mislead. If 79.7 percent is treated as the normal learner, the design may overlook older adults, low-income households or places where coverage exists but service is unstable.

Coverage and capability are separate layers. A signal permits connection; it does not supply a suitable device, affordable data, accessible interface or confidence in evaluating online information. Capability includes the practical knowledge and resources required to turn connection into purposeful action.

Generative AI makes this distinction sharper. By March 2025, 346 services had been registered, and AI applications were entering education as well as work and design. A learner who can open a chatbot may still struggle to frame a useful question, detect an unsupported claim or protect personal information.

Educational inclusion therefore requires more than extending a network. Schools, libraries and community centers can provide devices, guided practice and places to ask for help. Offline materials and low-bandwidth options remain important because infrastructure fails unevenly.

The digital divide is not one gap that closes when a cable arrives. It is a sequence of thresholds—connection, affordability, accessibility, skill and critical judgment. Policy succeeds when people can cross the whole sequence, not when the first threshold produces an impressive national percentage.

title: The Language Degree After Machine Translation
content:
Several Chinese universities have reduced or suspended admissions to foreign-language programs. Between 2018 and 2022, 109 institutions discontinued 28 language-related disciplines, with Japanese, English and Korean among the most affected. Employment data and changing institutional priorities contributed to the decisions, while machine translation and artificial intelligence altered the work graduates might perform.

It would be easy to read the adjustment as evidence that languages have lost value. The stronger interpretation is that language competence alone no longer defines a complete professional identity. Programs centered almost entirely on literature or translation technique may struggle when employers need people who can also understand law, finance, engineering or data.

Universities have responded with interdisciplinary combinations, including languages with law, journalism, computer science and AI. Interdisciplinary does not mean placing two course lists side by side. It means designing problems that require students to use knowledge from both fields—for example, evaluating the legal risk and cultural nuance of an automated translation used in an international contract.

Such reform carries two opposite dangers. If departments protect every old course, they may ignore real changes in work. If they chase each new technology, they may weaken the deep linguistic and cultural study that makes graduates more than operators of software. The correct balance is not fifty-fifty by credit count; it depends on the capabilities a program promises.

Program closure is also a blunt signal. Low enrollment may show weak demand, but it can reflect poor course design, regional need or inadequate career information. Before closing a small language, a university should ask whether its strategic value can be sustained through shared teaching or a combined degree.

Foreign-language education is therefore not disappearing so much as renegotiating its purpose. Its future lies in graduates who can interpret words, institutions and technologies together—and who understand what an automated system misses when it produces a fluent sentence.

title: AI Literacy Includes the Right to Say No
content:
An “AI Plus Education” action plan proposes a general AI-literacy system stretching from primary school through higher and vocational education to lifelong learning. Primary and secondary schools are asked to integrate AI into local curricula and activities. Universities should offer basic public courses and build interdisciplinary programs; vocational institutions should connect AI with traditional industries.

The word literacy matters. It should not be reduced to operating a popular application. AI literacy includes understanding what a system can do, recognizing uncertainty, testing claims, protecting data and deciding when automation is inappropriate. Functional use is one layer; critical and civic judgment are others.

The plan also extends to teachers. It calls for a national literacy standard, tiered training and assessment, and AI knowledge in qualification and certification processes. These measures can create a common floor. They cannot, by themselves, ensure that a teacher can redesign a history discussion, diagnose a misleading output or protect a vulnerable pupil in a real classroom.

Evidence from schools illustrates both reach and ambition. Beijing students receive at least eight hours of AI learning each academic year. One Shenzhen primary school reported monthly lessons for all 1,508 pupils. At Fudan University, more than 13,000 students had taken over 100 AI-related courses, and interdisciplinary dual-degree programs linked AI with other areas.

Numbers invite two mistaken conclusions. The first is that exposure equals competence. The second is that one standard must produce one identical curriculum. A national framework should specify transferable outcomes while allowing examples, tools and pacing to reflect age, discipline and local capacity.

Assessment must likewise move beyond button-pressing. Learners could be asked to compare two outputs, identify missing evidence, disclose assistance and explain why they accepted or rejected a recommendation. Such tasks make judgment visible.

A literacy system becomes inclusive not simply when a course exists at every stage, but when people can use, question and sometimes refuse AI with reasons they understand and can communicate.

title: Teaching the Chef Who Can Question the Robot
content:
A vocational program for future chefs introduced AI and stir-frying robots into two partner schools. More than 100 students studied technology trends, robot principles, practical operation and AI recipe development. Those who passed an assessment received an intelligent-chef certificate. The training responded to difficult kitchen conditions and an industry hiring gap reported at 10 million positions in 2023.

Automation in this setting is neither a simple enemy of craft nor a magical replacement for labor. A machine may repeat a temperature and motion consistently, reduce exposure to heat and handle routine production. A chef still judges ingredients, taste, timing, menu context and the expectations of diners. The educational problem is how to divide work without dividing knowledge.

If trainees learn only to press preset buttons, they become dependent on one model of equipment. If they study only traditional technique, they may enter workplaces already organized around sensors, data and standardized production. Hybrid competence means being able to perform, interpret and improve work across human and automated parts of a process.

Industry participation can keep courses current. The robotics company supplied training and certification, while a food company linked the program with culinary culture and employment needs. Yet partnership creates possible bias: a certificate designed by one provider may emphasize its product, and impressive efficiency claims may not capture maintenance costs, energy use or changes in food quality.

Schools therefore need independent learning outcomes. Students should be able to compare manual and automated methods, diagnose failure, adjust a recipe and explain safety decisions. They also need to understand how technology changes job roles, responsibility and the distribution of savings.

The reported robot was used by about 1,500 catering businesses, and one company claimed an 84 percent efficiency increase. Those figures justify attention, not surrender of judgment. Vocational education should prepare learners for the technology they will meet while giving them enough underlying knowledge to question, repair and improve it.

title: Four Questions Before a School Approves an AI Tool
content:
A 2025 guideline on generative AI in primary and secondary schools begins with age, not software popularity. Primary pupils should not independently use open-ended content generators. Middle school students may examine the logic of generated material, while high school students can undertake inquiry that includes technical principles. The progression is intended to protect cognitive development while allowing deeper responsibility over time.

The guideline also prohibits submitting generated content as original work, using AI to cheat and depending on it for creative tasks without critical thought. Teachers may use AI to assist planning or tutoring, but it should supplement rather than replace human-led teaching. Direct automated evaluation of students and processing sensitive personal data are restricted.

These rules illustrate why “permission” is too simple a policy category. A tool can be appropriate for one age, task and level of supervision but inappropriate for another. Age-appropriate use means matching both capability and risk to learnersʼ developing judgment; it is not a belief that every child of the same age is identical.

Schools are asked to establish data protection, ethical review and dynamic whitelists of approved tools. A whitelist can narrow obvious risk, yet approval must be revisable. Models change, terms of service shift and a safe general application may behave differently when connected to student records.

Academic integrity also requires better assessment design. If an assignment rewards a polished summary that software can produce instantly, surveillance alone will not restore learning. Teachers can ask students to show sources, compare versions, explain rejected suggestions or complete part of the reasoning in class. Such tasks make authorship and judgment visible.

Parental supervision is useful, especially for younger pupils, but responsibility should not be transferred entirely to families. Parents possess unequal technical knowledge and time. Schools and authorities still owe clear rules, approved alternatives and support when a learner or family chooses not to use a tool.

Human-centered does not mean keeping education unchanged. It means efficiency remains subordinate to development, privacy, fairness and meaningful teacher-student relationships. The strongest rule is not simply “use” or “do not use,” but a transparent answer to who may use what, for which learning purpose, under whose supervision and with what route to challenge harm.

title: Twenty-Three Tasks Need One Direction
content:
An education plan for 2026–2030 sets a broad objective: by the end of the period, China aims to have essentially completed a high-quality system and strengthened lifelong learning. Its 23 key tasks fall into five areas, including virtue, support for science and talent, public-service quality, teacher development and international opening.

The breadth is intentional, but it complicates accountability. When a policy links moral education, research capacity, demographic change, digital transformation and global influence, almost any activity can be described as relevant. A portfolio needs a theory of change: an explicit account of how particular actions are expected to produce stated outcomes and under what conditions.

Consider the planʼs call to align services with shifts in the school-age population. Fewer children in one district may justify consolidating facilities, while population inflow elsewhere requires new classrooms. A simple national pupil-teacher ratio could improve even as some families travel farther and fast-growing schools become crowded. Distributional evidence must accompany national totals.

The same issue appears in support for science, technology and human resources. Funding a new laboratory is observable immediately; the quality of inquiry it enables emerges later and depends on faculty, research culture and tolerance for uncertain results. If evaluation rewards quick outputs, institutions may select safe projects that contradict the planʼs ambition.

Teacher quality is another cross-cutting dependency. New curricula, inclusive public services and intelligent systems all ask teachers to learn additional roles. Training hours are an input. Whether teachers can diagnose misconceptions, adapt materials and collaborate across disciplines is a capability that needs observation and support.

Opening education internationally adds further tensions. Exchange can widen knowledge and networks, yet imported models require local interpretation. Global competitiveness should not turn cooperation into a narrow ranking contest.

A five-year plan becomes manageable when each task has a small number of credible indicators, a named responsible institution and scheduled review. Indicators should combine reach, quality and distribution, while qualitative evidence explains unexpected results.

Coherence is the final test. The five areas should reinforce rather than silently cancel one another. An education system is strong not because every objective appears in a document, but because decisions across funding, staffing and evaluation point toward the same public purposes.

title: A Global Platform Should Behave Like a Network
content:
A global AI education service platform was launched at the 2026 World Digital Education Conference in Hangzhou. It forms part of an upgrade to Smart Education of China, which was accessible in around 220 countries and regions. New international services included a lifelong-learning hub and a Chinese-language learning community.

Cross-border reach can reduce duplication. A country or institution may adapt high-quality material rather than build every resource from the beginning. Shared platforms can also connect teachers who face similar problems and make less widely taught subjects visible. Reach, however, is not the same as transfer.

Educational material carries assumptions about curriculum sequence, examples, language, bandwidth and the role of a teacher. A lesson that works in one system may arrive too early, rely on inaccessible cultural references or require devices unavailable elsewhere. Localization is not decorative translation; it is the redesign needed for a resource to function in another learning environment.

Governance becomes more difficult across borders. Learner data may pass through several legal jurisdictions. A recommendation model trained on one group may rank material poorly for another. Institutions need clarity about hosting, licensing, data retention, appeal and the ability to remove or correct content.

The launch initiative called for sharing high-quality resources and digital tools to bridge the global divide while supporting well-rounded, sustainable human development. These aims can conflict. Rapid expansion may favor dominant languages and easily measured subjects, while inclusive development requires investment in accessibility, local educators and small communities.

A global platform should therefore be evaluated as a network, not a warehouse. A warehouse counts items and visitors. A network examines relationships: who contributes, who adapts, whose feedback changes the system and whether less-resourced participants gain decision-making power.

Reciprocity is crucial. If knowledge travels mainly from a central provider outward, the service may reproduce hierarchy under the name of sharing. Regional institutions should be able to publish, revise and govern material, not merely consume it.

The achievement of a launch is connection. The educational achievement comes later, when resources cross borders without losing relevance, learners retain rights and participants on every side can shape what the platform becomes.

title: Equal Opportunity Is Not a Software Feature
content:
At the 2026 Global Smart Education Conference, experts argued that artificial intelligence should expand equal learning opportunities. The meetingʼs theme joined equity, quality and sustainability, while speakers called for cooperation, stronger teacher digital literacy and multilingual, accessible systems.

The three terms are easy to repeat and difficult to hold together. Equity asks who benefits and who bears risk. Quality asks whether learning becomes deeper or more reliable. Sustainability asks whether a service can be financed, maintained and governed over time without exhausting people or resources. A project can improve one dimension while damaging another.

For example, automated tutoring may offer additional practice to a remote learner. If it works only in a dominant language, it widens access for some while excluding others. Translating the interface is insufficient when examples, speech recognition or feedback still misunderstand local use. Multilingual design must enter data collection, evaluation and human support.

Teacher capacity is similarly structural. Training cannot consist only of learning where buttons are located. Educators need to identify bias, redesign tasks, verify claims and recognize when a learner requires human attention. If new systems increase monitoring and correction work without time or support, apparent efficiency transfers hidden labor to teachers.

International cooperation can share technical knowledge and reduce repeated mistakes, but borrowed solutions need national and local ownership. Countries differ in curriculum, infrastructure and law. Co-creation means that participants help define the problem and evaluate the result, not simply test a finished product designed elsewhere.

Sustainability also requires an exit question. What happens when a grant ends, a vendor changes terms or a model is withdrawn? Data portability, open standards, local technical skill and procurement safeguards can reduce dependence. They rarely appear in a classroom demonstration, yet they determine continuity.

An equity claim should therefore include disaggregated evidence. Average improvement may hide that rural learners, disabled students or speakers of minority languages gained less. The people most likely to be missed should be involved before deployment, not consulted only after harm appears.

AI can contribute to equal opportunity, but equality is not a property of the tool. It is an institutional achievement produced by inclusive design, capable teachers, durable governance and evidence that makes uneven outcomes visible.

title: What Eighteen Pupils Can Teach a System
content:
Laos began a research study on inclusive education for students with disabilities in the 2026–2027 school year. The work involved 18 pupils at a primary school in Xieng Khuang province and aimed to test a new classroom tool, strengthen teachersʼ methods and identify conditions for sustainable use.

The small scale is not a weakness if the purpose is learning before expansion. A pilot can reveal how a tool interacts with lesson routines, family involvement and district support. It becomes weak when participants are treated as a miniature version of the whole country and local findings are generalized without explanation.

The study uses several forms of evidence: classroom observation, teacher-completed forms, individual learning plans, monitoring data, interviews and focus groups. This mixture supports triangulation—the comparison of different evidence sources to see whether they point toward the same conclusion. A teacher report of increased participation, for instance, can be checked against observation and pupil work.

Inclusive education also complicates the definition of success. Reading and writing growth matter, but so do communication, confidence, attendance, social participation and a learnerʼs ability to ask for support. One standardized score may miss progress that changes a childʼs daily life. At the same time, warm stories cannot replace systematic evidence about who benefited and who did not.

Parental involvement is included because classroom change travels beyond school. Families may explain a childʼs communication, reinforce strategies or identify burdens created by a new routine. Yet involvement should not shift professional responsibility onto parents or disadvantage children whose caregivers have less time.

Implementation research must document context. Class size, teacher workload, accessible materials, specialist support and transport can determine whether a method is feasible. When the study is later used elsewhere, those conditions should travel with the reported result.

Ethics is especially important in a small group. Participants may be recognizable even when names are removed, and families may feel pressure to join a government-supported project. Clear consent, protected records and a route to decline without losing services are part of educational quality.

The most valuable result of the pilot may not be a verdict that the tool “works.” It may be a precise account of for whom it helped, through which teaching practices and with what support—knowledge that makes later expansion more careful and more genuinely inclusive.

title: Inclusion Begins Before a Child Enters the Room
content:
An inclusive kindergarten project in China allows children with intellectual and developmental disabilities to learn alongside peers without disabilities, with support and accommodation. Begun through cooperation between education authorities and UNICEF at the end of 2022, it had reached about 1.1 million children in 1,682 schools and kindergartens across seven provincial-level regions.

Individual stories show why placement can matter. Children who initially struggled to communicate, dress themselves or join routines learned by watching peers and through repeated teacher support. Their classmates also became more patient and willing to help. Inclusion, in these accounts, changes the social environment for everyone rather than moving one child into an unchanged room.

That distinction is essential. Physical presence is integration only in the narrowest sense. Educational inclusion requires accommodation: deliberate changes in communication, materials, routines or environment that enable participation without lowering the learnerʼs dignity. It also requires teachers who can notice different forms of progress.

The program exposes a resource tension. One reported class had sixteen children, three with special needs. A teacher can encourage peer support, but classmates must not become unpaid aides, and one childʼs access should not depend on another childʼs kindness. Specialist advice, planning time and manageable staffing turn goodwill into a reliable entitlement.

Benefits for peers should be described carefully. Greater empathy is valuable, yet children with disabilities are not placed in a classroom to provide moral lessons to others. Their own right to education remains primary. Likewise, a success story should not hide pupils whose needs require additional or different settings.

Transition is a critical test. Some children from the participating kindergartens entered public primary schools, but a supportive preschool year does not guarantee that accommodations continue. Records, family knowledge and specialist plans need to move with the child, while the receiving school must prepare before arrival.

National figures show progress: compulsory-education enrollment among children and adolescents with disabilities had reached 97 percent, and more than 30,000 students with disabilities entered universities each year. Enrollment, however, is the first link in a longer chain that includes attendance, participation, learning, belonging and progression.

Sustainable inclusion therefore depends on coordination among schools, families, health services, disability organizations and local authorities. It is not a favor offered by an unusually caring teacher. It is a systemʼs promise that difference will be anticipated, support will be organized and every learnerʼs development will remain visible.
